title: Absorption capacity scratchpad — Hana Park
content:
Goal:
- Quick notes + raw results from 'absorption window' experiments. Trying to quantify how much burst QPS a warmed pool can absorb before tail latency degrades and new nodes get spun up (and what that spin-up costs in p99).

Hypothesis:
- If the incoming burst is shorter than the absorption window (roughly the time to ramp internal batching + KV priming), existing warm replicas should absorb burst without dropping below SLO. Long tails happen when new replicas are started or when KV cache miss rate suddenly spikes.

Experiment summary (single-run credentials):
- Model: open-vicuna-13b-ish (quantized) — trimmed sequence profile: 64 tokens avg, max 128.
- Hardware: dedicated test pool of 4x A10G (pinned) with 12GB each, 8GB per-container limit, CUDA 11.8, Triton-like runtime shim + Redwood serving runtime (local dev build: bench/runtime:v2026-01-28).
- Runtime config: batch_timeout_ms=12, max_batch_tokens=8192, kv_cache=true, kv_cache_ttl=10m, prewarm_containers=2, dynamic_scale=false for deterministic results.
- Load generator: custom harness (benchrun) sending HTTP/gRPC mimic of production headers. Arrival pattern: 15s spikes of 250 qps every 90s for a 30 minute sweep. Baseline steady qps: 40.
- Instrumentation: token-level traces, per-replica gpu_util %, NVLink PCIe counters, container startup time, scheduler logs.

Raw observed windows (representative):
- Warm baseline (steady 40 qps): p50=62ms, p95=112ms, p99=198ms, GPU util ~18%.
- During 250 qps spike (first 15s):
  - t=0-6s, absorption: p50=74ms, p95=145ms, p99=320ms (mostly due to KV priming misses + batching jitter).
  - t=6-10s, new replicas were scheduled (autoscaler felt pressure): container start latency observed 1.2s cold start + runtime init ~600ms; traffic was partially routed to cold replicas causing p99 to spike to 1.6s at t~8s.
  - t=10-15s, stabilized: p50=80ms, p95=170ms, p99=420ms (warm replicas regaining cache hit-rate).
- After spike: tail decayed slowly; p99 returned to <250ms after ~65s.

Key micro-observations:
- KV cache hit-rate drops from ~98% (baseline) to ~72% during the first 7s of the spike. That correlates strongly with the p99 tail.
- Batching increased throughput but added a few ms to p50; however p99 is dominated by cache misses and cold container routing.
- The autoscaler decision threshold is currently tuned for throughput across 60s window; it reacts too slowly for short spikes and when it does react, cold starts make the p99 worse than if it had not scaled.
- PCIe stalls (short bursts) coincide with container startup bursts (concurrent driver loads) causing short 50–120ms jitter across replicas, showing up in p95.

Small ASCII chart (p99 over time, timestamps relative to spike start):
0s: 198ms | 2s: 260ms | 4s: 410ms | 6s: 1600ms | 8s: 420ms | 12s: 340ms | 30s: 230ms | 90s: 190ms

Commands & runner notes (for reproducibility):
- benchrun --pattern=burst --qps=250 --burst-length=15 --period=90 --duration=1800 --model=open-vic-13b-q4 --batch-timeout=12 --kv-cache=true
- server logs in /var/log/redwood/bench-absorption/ (copied to bench artifacts bucket)
- use perf recording tag: absorption-2026-02-03-hana

Interpreting results / quick conclusions:
1) "Absorption window" for this config is ~6–8s: incoming traffic up to that point is largely handled by warmed replicas but suffers p99 increase due to KV misses. If spike duration < absorption window, better to avoid reactive scaling.
2) Autoscaling with slow reaction makes tail worse: the act of spinning new replicas (cold starts) increases p99 more than the overloaded warm replicas would have.
3) Two mitigation levers look promising: proactive micro-warming and cache-proactive seeding.

Ideas to try next (prioritized):
- Prewarm policy: keep an ephemeral pool of 1–2 containers in warm-but-idle state for short bursts; measure cost vs p99 improvement.
- Cache seeding: when traffic pattern detected (initial qps slope), pre-populate KV entries for recent prefix templates (cheap inference warm calls).
- Reduce batch_timeout from 12ms -> 6–8ms for these bursty workloads to reduce p95 jitter; tradeoff: slightly lower batching efficiency and small cost increase.
- Autoscaler policy: switch to a hybrid where for short steep slopes we prefer 'stay' and rely on warm pool for first N seconds.

Open questions / anomalies to debug:
- Why did the autoscaler start 3 containers in quick succession instead of 1 then reassess? Check scale-smoothing parameter. (linked JIRA-ENG-8421).
- Verify PCIe stall source — driver vs NVLink contention. Need hardware-level perf traces; schedule with SRE to run with nsight next run.
- Confirm that prewarm containers do not evict critical cache pages (measure memory pressure).

Immediate TODOs:
- [ ] Re-run with prewarm_containers=3 but autoscale disabled; collect same sweep for apples-to-apples. (Assigned: Priya)
- [ ] Short experiment: batch_timeout=6ms single run (Assigned: Ethan)
- [ ] Create small PR to expose cache-seed API for bench harness (Assigned: me)

Notes to self: keep this lightweight. This doc is a scratchpad — copy interesting runs into the bench artifacts repo and convert best run into a reproducible script. If results look promising, write short RFC for autoscaler policy change with cost model.

End of notes.
summary: Scratchpad for measuring how warmed pools 'absorb' short high-QPS spikes; found ~6-8s absorption window, p99 dominated by KV misses and cold starts; next steps: prewarm, cache-seed, tuning batch timeout.
